q: Who is designated as the In-Flight Security Coordinator (ISC) for each flight?
a: The Pilot-in-Command (PIC) is designated as the ISC for each flight, responsible for the safety and security of the aircraft, guests, and crewmembers.

src.quote: The Pilot-in-Command (PIC) is designated as the ISC for each flight.
src.note: The ISC performs required duties per the applicable security program for the type of flight operated.

q: At what point is security responsibility transferred to the ISC?
a: Once an aircraft door closes, security responsibility is transferred to the ISC.

src.quote: Once an aircraft door closes, security responsibility is transferred to the ISC.
src.note: The ISC must review pertinent security information with the GSC for each flight segment before the transfer.

q: During what period must the Flight Deck Door be closed and locked under the Secure Flight Deck procedure?
a: From pushback (or engine start, if pushback is not required) until the aircraft has been brought to a stop at its final position on the ramp and the engines are shut down.

src.quote: The Flight Deck Door shall be closed and locked from pushback (or engine start, if pushback is not required) until the time the aircraft has been brought to a stop at its final position on the ramp and the engines are shut down.
src.note: Secure Flight Deck procedures are not required during Part 91 operations.

q: During the Secure Flight Deck period, for what four circumstances may the Flight Deck Door be opened?
a: To conduct a contamination check or perform MEL inspection; to allow a crewmember to attend to physiological needs; to deliver or remove meal service items; and with the Captain's specific approval.

src.quote: To conduct a contamination check or perform MEL inspection
src.note: The time the door is open shall be kept to a minimum, and all door opening and exiting procedures shall be followed.

q: Who is authorized access to the Flight Deck during Secure Flight Deck time?
a: Access is limited to Alaska Airlines crewmembers, Federal Inspectors, Secret Service, Federal Air Marshals, and those with specific authorization.

src.quote: Access to the Flight Deck during Secure Flight Deck time is limited to Alaska Airlines crewmembers, Federal Inspectors, Secret Service, Federal Air Marshals, and those with specific authorization
src.note: Specific authorization references Flight Deck Jumpseat Access procedures.

q: To how long should crewmembers strive to limit the time the Flight Deck Door is open?
a: Three seconds or less, because the Flight Deck is most vulnerable when the door is open.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.6.6 — Flight Deck Door Opening – Passenger Operations
src.quote: crewmembers should strive to limit the time the door is open to three seconds or less
src.note: If any threat is perceived while the door is open, any crewmember must loudly shout, “Door, Door, Door” to alert others to immediately close it.

q: What must any crewmember shout if a threat is perceived while the Flight Deck Door is open?
a: "Door, Door, Door" to alert other crewmembers to immediately close the Flight Deck Door.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.6.6 — Flight Deck Door Opening – Passenger Operations
src.quote: any crewmember must loudly shout, “Door, Door, Door” to alert other crewmembers to immediately close Flight Deck Door
src.note: Flight Deck Lockdown Procedures (15.3.13) are then followed if necessary.

q: If the Flight Crew receives a keypad activation warning signal, what must they assume?
a: Without any other information from the Flight Attendants, they must assume that a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack is in progress in the passenger cabin.

src.quote: they must assume, without any other information from the Flight Attendants, that a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack, is in progress in the passenger cabin
src.note: The keypad control device shall not be used for normal entry; entry attempts using the keypad shall be denied by the Flight Crew.

q: What is the minimum number of people that must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed after a crewmember exits?
a: A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.6.7 — Flight Deck Exit – Passenger Operations
src.quote: A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed
src.note: If a pilot and a jumpseater both need to leave, the “A” Flight Attendant/FFA (or designee) must enter the Flight Deck.

q: May medical personnel be given access to the Flight Deck?
a: No. Medical personnel shall not be given access to the Flight Deck.

src.quote: Medical personnel shall not be given access to the Flight Deck.
src.note: This applies even when MedLink or onboard medical personnel are assisting with a passenger.

q: May a KCM participant whose boarding pass shows SSSS use a KCM access point?
a: No. KCM participants with a boarding pass showing SSSS are not permitted to use KCM access points and must proceed to a standard passenger screening checkpoint.

src.quote: KCM participants with a boarding pass showing SSSS are not permitted to use KCM access points.
src.note: KCM participants also cannot bring other individuals, pets, or others' personal property through KCM access points.

q: Are uniformed crewmembers subject to the one carry-on plus one personal item limit, and what inspection are all their bags subject to?
a: Uniformed crewmembers, whether assigned to a flight or not, are not subject to the one carry-on bag plus one personal item limitation. All bags are subject to random Explosive Trace Detection (ETD) inspection.

src.quote: Uniformed crewmembers, whether assigned to a flight or not, are not subject to the limitation of one carry-on bag plus one personal item.
src.note: Crewmember baggage is not subject to random hand searches after clearing the x-ray unless an illegal or unexplained item is detected.

q: Who is permitted to carry a firearm on duty, and what personal protection devices are Flight Crew prohibited from carrying?
a: Only a Flight Crewmember authorized as a Federal Flight Deck Officer (FFDO) may carry firearms; otherwise the carriage of firearms or other weapons on duty or on Company property is prohibited. Flight Crew are also prohibited from carrying chemical irritating agents such as pepper spray (Mace).

src.quote: the carriage of firearms or other weapons while on duty or while on Company property is prohibited
src.note: The only exception is a Flight Crewmember authorized as an FFDO.

q: Whose ID does the CSA verify for a Federal Air Marshal team, and must the Flight Crew check FAM ID?
a: The FAM Team Lead provides ID to the CSA and advises of additional team members; the CSA only needs to verify the Team Lead's ID. The Flight Crew need not check ID, but if there is doubt as to identity, contact Dispatch via telephone, not the aircraft radio.

src.quote: The CSA only needs to verify the Team Lead's ID. The Flight Crew need not check ID
src.note: Do not transmit any communication regarding the FAM program via the radio.

q: What is the standing rule about taking off with a known passenger disturbance?
a: NEVER take off with a KNOWN passenger disturbance.

src.quote: NEVER take off with a KNOWN passenger disturbance.
src.note: If the situation escalates, consider contacting the local airport police for assistance.

q: How many high risk prisoners are allowed per flight and how many armed LEOs must accompany each?
a: Only one high risk prisoner is allowed per flight unless specifically approved in advance by TSA, and each prisoner must be accompanied by two or more armed LEOs who may not be responsible for any other prisoners.

src.quote: Only one high risk prisoner is allowed per flight, unless specifically approved in advance by TSA.
src.note: For low risk, one LEO may control two low risk prisoners on flights up to four hours; two LEOs are required for up to two low risk prisoners on flights over four hours.

q: Once the Flight Deck Door has been locked down in response to a Level 3 or Level 4 threat, may it be reopened?
a: No. The door shall not be reopened under any circumstances; declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable airport. During Levels 3 and 4 the Flight Attendants will also lockdown the cabin.

src.quote: the door shall not be reopened under any circumstances—declare an emergency, and land at the nearest suitable airport
src.note: For a Level 1 or Level 2 event, do not terminate lockdown restrictions until the F/As communicate the threat is resolved.

q: Which transponder code is used for hijacking, and may code 7700 be used during a hijacking?
a: Code 7500 is the unique code used for hijacking. Code 7700 shall not be used during a hijacking; that procedure has been eliminated from the common strategy.

src.quote: Code 7500 is the unique code used for hijacking.
src.note: Per 15.3.15.1, do not use code 7700 during a hijacking; ATC will normally ask for confirmation of a 7500 squawk only once due to concern over possible duress.

q: How many distinct passenger threat levels does Common Strategy identify, and what does each describe?
a: Four passenger threat levels: Level One is disruptive behavior, suspicious or threatening; Level Two is physically abusive behavior; Level Three is life-threatening behavior; and Level Four is attempted breach of the Flight Deck or actual breach.

src.quote: There are four passenger threat levels, developed by government and industry experts
src.note: They help identify the seriousness of suspicious or threatening activity occurring on board an aircraft.

q: After deplaning at a remote location for a credible bomb threat during taxiing, how far must the PIC move passengers and crew?
a: The PIC will direct passengers and crew to move at least 100 yards upwind of the aircraft and initiate a passenger and crew count; the GSC ensures ground personnel are at least 100 yards from the aircraft.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.19.2 — Credible IED/Bomb Threat – During Taxiing
src.quote: The PIC will direct the passengers and crew to move at least 100 yards upwind of the aircraft
src.note: An aircraft with a credible bomb threat may never be taxied to the gate until the NOC/SOCC deems the threat terminated.

q: SCENARIO (Flight Deck Door discipline): In cruise, the First Officer opens the Flight Deck Door to step out per the exit procedure. As the door swings open, a passenger near the forward galley suddenly lunges toward the aisle. What is the required immediate action, and what is the door-open time target?
a: Any crewmember who perceives the threat must loudly shout "Door, Door, Door" to alert other crewmembers to immediately close the Flight Deck Door, then follow Flight Deck Lockdown Procedures (15.3.13) if necessary. Crewmembers strive to keep the door open three seconds or less because the Flight Deck is most vulnerable when the door is open.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.6.6 — Flight Deck Door Opening – Passenger Operations
src.quote: If any threat is perceived while Flight Deck Door is open, any crewmember must loudly shout, “Door, Door, Door” to alert other crewmembers to immediately close Flight Deck Door.
src.note: The Flight Deck is most vulnerable when the door is open, so crewmembers should strive to limit the time the door is open to three seconds or less.

q: SCENARIO (jumpseat / two-person rule): You are the Captain. Your First Officer and the flight-deck jumpseater both need to leave the Flight Deck at the same time. What must occur before both can step out?
a: A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed. Because a pilot and the jumpseater both need to leave, the "A" Flight Attendant/FFA (or designee) must enter the Flight Deck to hold the number at two. The second person closes and secures the door and follows Flight Deck Reentry Procedures when the crewmember returns.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.6.7 — Flight Deck Exit – Passenger Operations
src.quote: If a pilot and the jumpseater both need to leave, the “A” Flight Attendant/FFA (or designee) must enter the Flight Deck.
src.note: A minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed; if a jumpseater remains, the F/A does not need to enter.

q: SCENARIO (threat level response): In cruise you receive a keypad activation warning signal, with no other communication from the Flight Attendants. What must the Flight Crew assume, and once locked down at that level, may the door be reopened?
a: Without any other information from the Flight Attendants, the Flight Crew must assume a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack is in progress in the passenger cabin. Once locked down in response to a Level 3 or Level 4 threat, the door shall not be reopened under any circumstances; declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable airport.

src.quote: If the Flight Crew receives a keypad activation warning signal they must assume, without any other information from the Flight Attendants, that a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack, is in progress in the passenger cabin.
src.note: Per 15.3.13, once locked down for a Level 3 or 4 threat the door shall not be reopened under any circumstances—declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable airport.

q: SCENARIO (armed LEO notification): Armed Individuals are already continuing through on your aircraft, and additional Armed Individuals are joining for the next segment. What must be completed before the aircraft door(s) can be closed?
a: All notifications must be made to the assigned crew and all Armed Individuals before the door(s) can be closed. The gate agent must inform each AI of the location of the others who are armed, including FAMs, and communications between Flight Crew, Flight Attendants, and AIs should be as discreet as possible.

src.ref: FOM 15.2.8 — Armed Individuals (other than FAM and FFDO)
src.quote: If AIs are joining a flight where AIs are continuing through, all notifications must be made to the assigned crew and all AIs before the door(s) can be closed.
src.note: The gate agent must inform the AI of the location of others who are armed, including FAMs; communications should be as discrete as possible.
